verdicts.trueWording: The descriptive passages are marvelous - you can smell the spice
verdicts.note: Levinson blog (Tangent #16, Fall 1996 repost, posted 22 Mar 2011) reads: 'The descriptive passages are marvelous - you can smell the spice, and taste it in every cup of wine Martin renders - but the story as a whole is not special.' Quote verbatim; page spells it 'marvelous'. Raw HTML fetched with a browser UA.

verdicts.trueWording: its superbly developed characters, accomplished prose and sheer bloody-mindedness
verdicts.note: PW page (Reviewed on: 07/29/1996) reads: 'the book stands out ... by virtue of its superbly developed characters, accomplished prose and sheer bloody-mindedness.' Quote verbatim; 1996 trade-review date confirmed on page.

verdicts.trueWording: no development ... no progression ... no climax; banging an endless series of chords
verdicts.note: Hilliard (post titled 'A Song of Ice and Fire 1 - 4', August 14, 2010): 'There is no development, there is no sense of progression of any kind, there is no climax. It's the plot equivalent of someone banging an endless series of chords, each unrelated to the next, on a piano.' Quote verbatim. Scope note: the sentence is aimed at the main 'game of thrones' thread, which he calls most of the series through 'the end of the fourth book', and he adds that the other plotlines are 'even further behind'.

verdicts.trueWording: more than any author I can recall, he has constructed a social landscape
verdicts.note: Hilliard: 'Martin's efforts in geographical construction and detail are merely adequate. Instead, more than any author I can recall, he has constructed a social landscape.' Quote verbatim; the people-not-physical-description limb is explicitly the page's own contrast.

verdicts.trueWording: I primarily associated ... intrigue and realism over magic and elevated prose
verdicts.note: Quote is verbatim on the page, but it sits inside the reviewer's PRE-READING expectation: 'from countless asides in conversations with friends and reviews of other books, I primarily associated two attributes with Martin's work: First, an unromantic approach to fantasy that emphasized intrigue and realism over magic and elevated prose.' He then writes 'the series Martin wrote was quite a bit different than the one I had expected to read' and, on grit and realism, 'Compared to Joe Abercrombie ... Martin seems like a hopeless romantic.' The page therefore does not assert this as the series' actual approach.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the claim asserts as the series' approach what the page gives as the reviewer's pre-reading expectation and then partly walks back

verdicts.trueWording: giving each character a clearly titled chapter solves the problem admirably
verdicts.note: Editorial Department page (stamped 2024-01-07T00:17:06+00:00, by Shannon Roberts): 'While shifting POV can occasionally lead to confusion, giving each character a clearly titled chapter solves the problem admirably.' Quote verbatim; both limbs on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: a swift pace and plenty of action ... three key points of conflict
verdicts.note: Same page: 'Martin's work is masterful-a swift pace and plenty of action are used to introduce the novel's three key points of conflict (the Night's Watch, Daenerys, and Ned's becoming the Hand).' Quote verbatim; the piece is explicitly a 'first 50' review of the first fifty pages.

verdicts.trueWording: By keeping the magic to small, measured doses, Martin maintains an air of suspense
verdicts.note: Same page: 'By keeping the magic to small, measured doses, Martin maintains an air of suspense that many fantasy novels risk losing within the first 50 pages.' Quote verbatim.

verdicts.trueWording: many individual chapters good enough to function on their own as award-worthy short stories
verdicts.note: SFF180 (Thomas M. Wagner, A Dance with Dragons): quote appears verbatim. Page qualifies with 'many individual chapters'; the claim's unqualified 'Individual chapters' reads as the same general point, no stronger.

verdicts.trueWording: like a filmmaker, he writes chapters out of order, and then sequences them later
verdicts.note: Quote verbatim on the page: 'Martin has said in interviews (or at least in one convention interview I sat in on) that, like a filmmaker, he writes chapters out of order, and then sequences them later.' The page's simile is 'filmmaker', not 'film editor'; it also attributes the practice to Martin's own interview remarks rather than stating it in the reviewer's own voice.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'like a film editor' - the page says 'like a filmmaker'

verdicts.trueWording: never meets anything less than the highest standards of literary craft
verdicts.note: SFF180: 'Martin's writing, as expected, never meets anything less than the highest standards of literary craft.' Quote verbatim; 'never meets anything less than' = the claim's 'never falls below'.

verdicts.trueWording: Martin's uncanny prose style contains a detailed realism that brings Tyrion to life on the page
verdicts.note: National Review live URL returned HTTP 403 to a browser UA; recovered via Wayback raw capture https://web.archive.org/web/20250617080036id_/... - body text lives inside a JSON payload in the page source. Sentence appears verbatim (curly apostrophe).

verdicts.trueWording: coarsely obsessed with politics, to the exclusion of almost everything else
verdicts.note: Same Wayback capture: 'to describe Tyrion is also pretty much to describe this first book - and Martin's entire saga: coarsely obsessed with politics, to the exclusion of almost everything else (except for occasional bouts of sex and/or violence).' Quote verbatim; every limb on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: fantasy as a backdrop or window dressing for ... a type of bloated Agatha Christie plotline
verdicts.note: Same capture: 'Martin's revealed preference is instead to use fantasy as a backdrop or window dressing for what is essentially a type of bloated Agatha Christie plotline.' Whodunit limb: 'Much of A Game of Thrones's plot centers on a "whodunit" mystery'. Goes-nowhere limb: 'the assassination plotline goes nowhere as the reader witnesses the characters become practically amnesiac about it'.

verdicts.trueWording: the book becomes predictable as the reader grows accustomed to ... cynical Machiavellianism
verdicts.note: Same capture: 'the way the book becomes predictable as the reader grows accustomed to interpreting every event through a lens of cynical Machiavellianism'. Quote verbatim; both limbs on the page.
